title: Microbial Growth and Its Control
lead: Microbiologists may need to grow microbes to detect them, use them as experimental models, or isolate molecules such as antibiotics and enzymes. Microbiologists may also need to kill or inactivate microbes to decontaminate spaces and treat infected subjects. Thus, microbiologists should know how microbes grow in natural environments and how to grow them in the laboratory. If the growth conditions of a microbe are known, those conditions can be manipulated to control microbial growth more efficiently. Safety is the central concern of the allied health professions. Healthcare professionals must protect themselves, their families, and their clients from infection risks at all times. For these reasons, allied health care professionals should be highly knowledgeable about disinfection, antisepsis, and personal protection. This chapter initially addresses microbial growth and finishes with the control of microbial growth in the environment. Despite all efforts to control them, microbial infections are inevitable. Treating microbial infections will be covered in Chapter 8. Part 1: Microbial Growth Subcellular and unicellular microbes grow by number but not by size, because the size of the parent and progeny is about the same. In contrast, multicellular metazoan organisms grow in both number (through reproduction) and size, from a single cell (zygote) about 50 micrometers to a larva or embryo (measured in centimeters) to an adult (which can be measured in centimeters to meters).

sections.heading: How microbes grow in natural environments

blocks.text: Almost all microbes can be considered aquatic organisms because they quickly desiccate in open terrestrial environments and are damaged by UV radiation. Thus, microbes generally grow in water, near an adequate moisture supply, or within the host body or cell.

Traditionally, microbial growth was studied in the laboratory, one species at a time. In natural environments, many microbial species live in communities, where some are producers (e.g., photosynthetic organisms that produce organic compounds), some are consumers (e.g., organisms that get nutrients from producers and other consumers as predators or parasites), and some are decomposers (e.g., organisms that recycle nutrients from dead organisms). All pathogenic microbes are predators, parasites, or decomposers. In this chapter, we will discuss the growth of mostly the pathogenic microbes.
Aquatic environments

Microbes in the aquatic environment may live as plankton (motile organisms that drift with water currents) or adhere to floating objects or the bottom substratum. Planktonic microbes are usually flagellated and may contain an air bubble for buoyancy. Microbes that adhere to a substratum usually create a biofilm. Oral bacteria from biofilm on teeth (dental plaque). Microbes in the large intestine form a biofilm on undigested food remnants. Bloodborne bacteria may also form biofilms on inanimate substances in the body, such as pacemakers and venous catheters. Many microbes, such as sulfur bacteria and some methane-producing archaea, grow deeper inside the bottom mud.

The common waterborne pathogens include viruses (such as norovirus, rotavirus, astrovirus, and hepatitis A and E viruses); bacteria (genera Vibrio, Pseudomonas, Legionella, Burkholderia, Aeromonas, and Escherichia, Salmonella, Shigella, Serratia, Klebsiella, and some species of Mycobacterium) (Fig. 7.1), protozoa (such as the genera Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Giardia, Naegleria, Entamoeba, and Balantidium); and fungi (such as some species of the genera Alternaria, Aspergillus and Fusarium). Some aquatic bacteria (such as Legionella pneumophyla) infect aquatic protozoa (amoebae). Ingestion of the infected amoebae transfers the pathogen to the human body. Aquatic larvae of some flatworms (for example, the genus Schistosoma) penetrate human skin before they enter the bloodstream. Eggs and larvae of some worms, such as the Guinea worm (Dracunculus mediensis), infect aquatic arthropods. Accidental ingestion of the infected arthropods transmits the worm eggs to humans. Some of the aquatic pathogens may also thrive in moist soil. Enteric bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella normally reside in the intestines of animals and humans. They can survive in natural waterbodies for a short time. The presence of E. coli in water indicates that human or animal waste has been released into the water.

Soil

Soil is made of fine rock particles and organic molecules, mainly plant materials (known as humus). Soil lacking organic materials is sand. There are air and water channels between the soil particles. Microbes usually grow attached to the rock particles. Organic-rich, well-drained, moist soil can contain as many as a billion microbial cells per gram of soil. Excess water floods the air capillaries of soil and drastically reduces biodiversity. Polluted soil and water (see Chapter 15) are also poor in biodiversity. Soil-borne pathogens include bacteria (genera Bacillus, Clostridium, Clostridioides, Burkholderia, Nocardia, Actinomyces, Streptomyces, and Listeria), protozoa (such as the genus Acanthamoeba), and fungi (genera Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Histoplasma, and Cryptococcus). Larvae of many nematode worms (including the hookworm larvae) enters human body from soil. Eggs and larvae of some flatworms (such as Taenia solium), and nematodes (such as the Genera Enterobius, Trichinella, Ascaris, and Toxocara) enter the human body through soiled food or accidental ingestion of contaminated soil. Fungal hyphae, nitrogen-fixing bacteria, and tree roots create an extensive network of living cells/tissues in soil. Worms and arthropods are also plentiful in soil.
Air

Wind flow can cause microbes attached to soil particles to become airborne and aerosolize aquatic microbes. Floating dust and aerosol particles may travel for many miles. Microbes on dust particles have been collected 10 km above the Earth's surface. Airborne soil microbes from Africa crossing the Atlantic Ocean and from China crossing the Pacific Ocean have been recorded. Airborne dust and microbe particles in the upper atmosphere contribute to the formation of raindrops and clouds.

Humans and animals release microbes through breathing and sneezing as droplets of diverse sizes (see Chapter 11). The droplets may stay airborne for a few minutes to a few hours. Microbes (bacteria and bacterial and fungal spores) in the ground-level air are plentiful. This can be proven by exposing a blood agar to room air for a few hours and then incubating at 35 oC overnight (Fig. 7.2). Air in dusty cities and areas near solid waste disposal contains high loads of microbes, which can be sampled and quantified using an air sampler (Fig. 7.2). Contaminated air is the primary source of respiratory infections and some other diseases.

Airborne pathogenic microbes include viruses (influenza virus, parainfluenza virus, rhinovirus, coronaviruses, measles virus, mumps virus, varicella zoster virus, adenovirus, and respiratory syncytial virus), bacteria (of the genera Legionella, Mycobacterium, Bordetella, Corynebacterium, Neisseria, Coxiella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, and Chlamydophila), and fungi (of genera Aspergillus, Mucor, Rhizopus, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Cladosporium, and Penicillium). The water and air of countries where human waste is not properly disposed of are heavily contaminated with microbes. Even nematode worm eggs have been sampled from the air in some of those countries. Human body Normal microbiotas reside in the skin, the eyes, the nasal cavity, the oral cavity, the pharynx, the middle and outer ear, the large intestine, the lower urethra, and the vagina of healthy individuals. The upper respiratory tract, stomach, small intestine, ureter, and bladder may contain a few bacteria in some subjects. Some primary pathogens can also colonize on those surfaces without causing disease. Humans are the only reservoir of sexually transmitted microbial agents (including viruses such as herpes simplex virus-1 and 2, human papillomavirus, and human immunodeficiency virus-1 and 2; bacterial pathogens Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Treponema pallidum, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, and Haemophilus ducreyi; and protozoan pathogens such as Trichomonas vaginalis. Human pathogens exit the body via dead skin cells, scabs, oral/nasal aerosols, blood from wounds, genital secretions, urine, and stool, and are transmitted to other humans (see Chapter 11).

blocks.text: Cellular organisms grow best when all the factors that affect their growth are present at their optimum levels. Non- cellular microbes, such as viruses and subviral agents, grow if their host cells grow optimally. The growth of all cellular microbes is affected by physical, chemical, and biological factors, as summarized below.

blocks.text: Physical factors, including temperature, light, pressure, sound waves, gravitation, water flow, and air currents, affect microbial growth. For pathogenic microbes, temperature is the most important factor. Temperature affects enzyme structure and the rate of chemical reactions. Cellular microbes are grouped as psychrophiles (cold-loving), psychrotrophs (cold-preferring), mesophiles (loving moderate temperatures, which is also the human body temperature), thermophiles (heat-loving), and hyperthermophiles (loving extreme heat), based on their optimum growth temperature and the range of temperatures they can survive (Table 7.1). All pathogenic microbes are either psychrotrophs or mesophiles. Mesophiles (such as E. coli) do not grow in refrigerators, but psychrotrophs (such as Listeria monocytogenes) do, which is a concern when consuming refrigerated food. Light is important for photosynthetic microbes, but none of them is pathogenic.

Water

Water is abundant in cells and the Earth's crust. Microbes rapidly desiccate when exposed to air, in the absence of water. Thus, the removal of water (drying, pickling, etc.; see Part 2 of this Chapter) is a major means of controlling microbes. Dissolved chemicals in water alter osmotic pressure, pH, and ion strength (ion concentration), thereby affecting microbial growth.
Osmotic pressure

The salt concentration in human body fluids is about 0.9% (about 295 milliosmole/kg), which is optimal for pathogenic microbes. Bacteria and fungi may survive in pure water (salt concentration < 0.5%) because they possess robust cell walls. Protozoan parasites survive in pure water by actively pumping water out of the cells. However, all microbial pathogens suffer crenation (shrinkage of cells lacking a cell wall) or plasmolysis (collapse of the cytoplasm of cells with a cell wall) due to water loss, leading to cell collapse at higher salt concentrations. A few bacterial pathogens, such as the genera Vibrio and Escherichia, survive in brackish water (salt concentration 0.5-3%). In general, brine (salt concentration 3.5-10%) inhibits the growth of most microbes, except obligate halophiles (salt-loving bacteria and archaea), but none of them are pathogenic.
pH

The pH of human body fluids is shown in Table 7.2. Since pH affects enzyme structure and function, microbes survive only within a narrow pH range. Pathogenic cellular microbes usually prefer a normal pH (about 7.0), but a few survive at extreme pH values. For example, Helicobacter pylori thrives in the stomach at pH 1.0-3.5, and E. coli survives in urine and blood (pH 3.5-7.5). Many microbes cannot grow in fermented foods due to the low pH created by lactic acid and other organic acids. Some acidophile (acid-loving) prokaryotes grow in sulfuric acid pools (pH about 3.0), while some alkaliphile (base-loving) prokaryotes thrive in soda lakes (pH about 12), but none of those are pathogenic.

Body fluid Range of pH Blood 7.31-7.45 Gastric juice 1.0-3.5 Saliva 6.2-7.5 Sweat 4.0-6.8 Urine 4.5-8.0 Vaginal fluid 3.8-4.5 Oxygen Aerobes use oxygen for cellular respiration (see Chapter 4). Obligate aerobes (such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae) cannot use other terminal electron acceptors. Thus, anaerobic conditions would kill them. However, facultative anaerobes (such as E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Salmonella enterica, Staphylococcus aureus, and Listeria monocytogenes) use oxygen if available, or an alternative terminal electron acceptor for respiration, or ferment if oxygen is unavailable. Obligate anaerobes (such as the genera Actinomyces, Clostridium, Bacteroides, Prevotella, and Fusobacterium) and obligate fermenters (such as Streptococcus pyogenes and Lactobacillus bulgaricus) thrive by fermenting.

Some obligate anaerobes (such as the genus Clostridium) are killed when exposed to air (oxygen). However, some obligate fermenters, such as Lactobacilli, survive in the presence of oxygen. Oxygen is a powerful oxidizing agent. Catabolic reactions involving oxygen generate some powerful reactive chemicals (free radicals) such as superoxide (O2-), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and singlet oxygen (1O2). These chemical substances can react with nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids, damaging these molecules. Aerobes, facultative anaerobes, and some obligate fermenters have chemical compounds, such as antioxidants (agents that prevent oxidation), and specific enzymes to help prevent such damage. The antioxidants include glutathione, carotene, and vitamins A and C. The enzymes that detoxify the reactive chemicals include superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and peroxidase. SOD neutralizes singlet oxygen by the reaction 2O2- + 2H+ à H2O2 + O2 Catalases and peroxidases detoxify H2O2 by the reactions 2H2O2 à 2H2O + O2 H2O2 + NADH + H+ à 2H2O +NAD+ Some pathogens (such as Helicobacter pylori and Neisseria gonorrhoeae) require oxygen for respiration but lack an enzyme to detoxify the free radicals. These organisms are called microaerophilic organisms; excess oxygen can kill them.

We previously discussed (in Chapter 4) that cellular microbes require 25 elements, a carbon source, and an electron source. Autotrophs use light energy to extract electrons from water or other inorganic compounds, while heterotrophs use organic chemicals (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, etc.) as the electron source (see Chapter 4). A few microbes (such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and E. coli) are prototrophs (can synthesize all the necessary organic molecules), but most pathogenic microbes are auxotrophs (depend on other organisms for certain organic molecules, such as vitamins and amino acids). This information helps grow microbes in a laboratory and control their growth. Limiting factors A limiting factor is a physical, chemical, or biological factor that restricts microbial growth, regardless of the abundance of other factors. For example, obligate aerobes cannot grow irrespective of the richness of the medium if oxygen is absent. Microbiologists manipulate the limiting factors to control microbes, both in the environment and within the human body.
Biological factors

As previously described, no organism in the biosphere is self-sufficient. Different species have slightly different gene sets, which give them distinct metabolic capacities. All species in the community, through their different roles, sustain the community biologically. The interdependence is so intense that most microbes (>99%) cannot be grown in the laboratory. Research has shown that one species uses another's metabolic waste products in natural environments, a phenomenon that is difficult to generate under laboratory conditions. Fortunately, most pathogenic microbes can be grown in the laboratory

blocks.text: Microbiologists grow viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and worms for various reasons, including diagnostic and research purposes. Growing viruses also requires growing the host cells/organisms. Growing (or culturing) cellular microbes in the laboratory requires a sterile growth medium (media guaranteed free of live microbes). The sterile medium is inoculated with the target microbes (usually a pure culture), and the culture is protected from any other contaminating microbes. This practice is called the aseptic technique.
Standard aseptic techniques

Standard aseptic techniques for microbiology laboratories include practices that ensure: (a) the culture medium must be kept sterile, (b) the laboratory bench surfaces should be clean, (c) microbes from the body of laboratory workers should not contaminate the workspace or the culture media, (d) microbes from the workspace must not enter the body surfaces of the laboratory workers, (e) microbial cultures must be protected from contaminating microbes, and (f) biohazard wastes (any item potentially contaminated with microbes) must be appropriately disposed of. A clearer understanding of aseptic techniques will develop after studying this chapter and the next (Chapter 6). Growth media A growth medium (also called a culture medium) is a mixture of nutrients necessary for growing an organism. Microbiologists have developed generic and species-specific culture media for many pathogenic and nonpathogenic microbes (see Difco BBL Manual, Difco Laboratories, Franklyn Lane, NJ). Here we will discuss media for growing bacteria, fungi, protozoa, worms, and mammalian cells.
Broth vs. semisolid media

In general, culture media are mixtures of nutrients in a buffered solution, known as broth. Broth is used for large- scale microbial culture. However, separating cellular microbes requires a semisolid medium. A semisolid medium is a broth containing 0.25-1.90 % agar. Agar is a mixture of polysaccharides derived from marine red algae, such as the genera Gelidium and Gracilaria. Agar is an ideal solidifying agent because a few microbes can digest it as a food source.
Chemically defined vs. complex media

A chemically defined medium contains pure chemical compounds (such as glucose and NaCl) of known chemical composition (Table 7.3). Only prototrophs can grow on such a medium. The medium can be manipulated to isolate auxotrophs and mutant prototrophs that require a specific organic molecule (supplement) to grow. A complex medium contains a mixture of pure chemical compounds and complex nutrients of unknown chemical composition, such as peptone (lean protein boiled and partially digested by proteolytic enzymes), tryptone (milk proteins partially digested by proteolytic enzymes), and yeast extract (broken yeast cells partially digested by endogenous enzymes). How to establish a pure culture of a prokaryote or fungus A pure culture contains only one strain or species of an organism. Since all microbes in the environment live in communities, a microbe cannot be biologically characterized unless a pure culture is established. To establish a pure culture, a loop that has touched a broth culture is streaked onto a semisolid medium, such as an agar plate (Fig. 7.4). Alternatively, a small volume of diluted culture is mixed with warm (40 oC) liquid agar and then poured on a plate (Fig. 7.4). Many species of bacteria, archaea, and fungi create distinct colonies on the plate. A colony is assumed to have developed from the growth of a single cell, more precisely, a colony-forming unit (CFU). However, the initial colony can contain two or more species. Streaking a few times using a well-isolated colony ensures a pure culture. Some microbes cannot grow in semisolid media but may grow in liquid media. A pure culture of such an organism can be tentatively established by counting cells/mL and then diluting the culture so that 1 mL of the culture medium contains 0-0.3 cells. One ml of the culture is then transferred to a new vessel to initiate a tentative pure culture.

blocks.text: When a pure culture of a microbe (a bacterium, yeast (fungus), or protozoan) is added to a broth culture, the cells initially do not grow. This step, called the lag phase (Fig. 7.5), is when the cell acclimatizes to the new environment and expresses proper genes to survive there. The cells then grow by binary fission at a fixed time interval known as the doubling time. The number of cells can be determined by taking a small sample, growing it in a semisolid medium, and counting the colonies.

The doubling continues as long as the medium contains adequate nutrients and no toxic waste products. This phase of growth is the log or exponential phase. At this phase, cells synthesize primary metabolites (such as amino acids, RNAs, and proteins) necessary for normal growth.

As the number of cells increases and nutrients are depleted, some cells die. At some point, the rate of cell growth equals the rate of cell death. This phase is known as the stationary phase. If fresh medium is added to the flask, the cells return to log phase, but then back to the stationary phase when the nutrients are depleted. Microbiologists may use a bioreactor to continuously add fresh nutrients and remove a small volume of cells to maintain a permanent log- phase culture.

During the stationary phase, cells begin producing secondary metabolites, such as antibiotics and toxins, to outcompete other cells. In addition, dead cells release cellular waste products into the medium. The toxic condition causes the death rate to exceed the growth rate. This step, known as the death or decline phase, continues for a while. Only mutated cells that can survive the toxic environment survive before the population completely collapses (Fig. 7.5).

In pristine natural environments, microbes grow continuously in the log phase because the nutrient supply is constant, predators and parasites continually remove some cells, and waste materials are recycled. The microbial count on a clean lake or a healthy human subject's body surfaces remains nearly constant for this reason. Death and detachment of epithelial cells covering the body, urination, defecation, showering, toothbrushing, and other hygienic practices prevent excessive microbial growth. However, environmental changes, such as higher temperatures and sudden nutrient surges (e.g., leakage of municipal waste into the local lake), may cause excessive microbial growth, leading to a stationary phase followed by a decline.
Fig. 7.5. An idealized growth curve of E. coli in a flask of growth medium. Different growth phases are indicated.

Note that the number of viable cells and the concentration of primary metabolites paralleled. Adding fresh nutrients after a stationary phase initiated a new log phase. Secondary metabolites gradually accumulate with time.

sections.heading: Growing selected pathogenic microbes in the laboratory

blocks.text: Growing bacteria

Microbiologists have developed many different types of growth media that help enrich, isolate, identify, and characterize different bacteria. A microbiologist could cleverly design growth media for different purposes. Growth media could be roughly grouped into the following categories: Selective media They suppress unwanted microbes and encourage the growth of desired microbes. Example: bismuth sulfite agar. Here, bismuth sulfite inhibits G(+) bacteria and most enteric bacteria but allows the growth of Salmonella enterica. Differential media They promote the growth of many species, but each species produces a distinct colony structure. Example: Blood agar plates where alpha-hemolytic species (of Streptococcus) produce green colonies, beta-hemolytic species clear the blood pigments and produce transparent colonies, and gamma-hemolytic species produce white colonies (Fig. 7.6). Selective-differential media They suppress unwanted species and allow surviving species to form different colony morphologies. Example: MacConkey agar; it suppresses G(+) bacteria while enteric bacteria (such as Escherichia and Salmonella) grow, forming colonies of different colors (Fig. 7.6 Selective-enrichment media Custom-designed for different species, for example, a medium with crude oil as the only carbon source to isolate a bacterium that can degrade crude oil in polluted soil (Fig. 7.6).
Maintenance media
These are nonselective media (for example, LB broth, blood agar, potato dextrose agar, etc.) that support the growth of diverse species and are used to maintain them in pure culture.
Growing fastidious bacteria

These are custom-designed media with added nutrients for pathogenic bacteria that have lost the ability to synthesize some essential molecules, such as vitamins. Example: chocolate agar medium for the cultivation of Francisella tularensis (Fig. 7.6).

Enrichment medium: Crude oil agar plate: one unknown species grew, forming white colonies. D. Specialty medium: Chocolate agar (containing boiled sheep blood) that allows the fastidious bacterium Francisella tularensis to grow. Image courtesy: Wikipedia.

Microaerophilic bacteria (such as Helicobacter pylori) grow in reduced oxygen, and capnophile (CO2-loving) bacteria (such as Campylobacter jejuni) grow in a reduced-oxygen/high CO2 atmosphere. Such an environment can be created inside a Candle Jar (Fig. 7.7). The inoculated plates are placed in a lidded jar, and a candle is burned inside to remove oxygen and generate excess CO2.

Strict anaerobes, such as Clostridium botulinum, cannot grow in the presence of molecular oxygen. To grow them, dissolved oxygen in the media is removed by adding sodium thioglycolate, and the plates are incubated in oxygen- free (i.e., replaced by nitrogen) incubators (Fig. 7.7)
Fig. 7.7. Growing fastidious bacteria. A. A candle jar for growing microaerophiles or capnophiles. B. An oxygen-

free workstation with gloved sleeves (figure courtesy of Terra Universal.com). C. A Vacu-Quick Jar is used for growing strict anaerobes. A pouch containing oxygen-removing chemicals removes oxygen from the jar's air. Figure courtesy of Almore Inc., Portland, OR.
Growing fungi

The methodologies of growing fungi and bacteria are similar. Fungal media (Table 7.3) are made from simple materials such as potato starch, cornmeal, carrot powder, and sucrose. The pH of fungal media is acidic, and antibiotics such as gentamicin are added to prevent bacterial growth. In agar plates, yeasts (single fungal cells) generally produce colonies like those of bacteria (Fig. 7.8). Molds produce thread-like hyphae inside and on top of the semisolid medium (Fig. 7.8).
Growing algae

Photosynthetic freshwater algae (such as Chlorella sp.) can be grown in autoclaved pond water supplemented with algal nutrients (SSD 1+2, Health Algae, Uppsala, Sweden), in a jar placed near a light source (Fig. 7.8). Some algae grow on agar plates supplemented with algal nutrients.
Fig. 7.8. Growing eukaryotic microbes. A. Yeast (Candida albicans) colonies on a Sabouraud-dextrose agar plate.

Photo: Ken Slater. B. Phoma herbarum, a mold, growing on a potato-dextrose agar plate. Photo: Ken Slater. C. Paramecium aurelia growing in a jar containing straw broth, with Klebsiella aerogenes as the food organisms. Photo: Nahid Kuddus. D. Chlorella vulgaris (a green alga) growing in a plastic bottle containing an algal growth medium. Image courtesy: Wikimedia. E. Paramecium caudatum, a protozoan (10x). Photo courtesy: VWR. F. Caenorhabditis elegans, a nematode worm, growing on a lawn of E. coli on an agar plate. Photo courtesy: http://www.nematodes.org. G. Phage plaques on a lawn of Pseudomonas aeruginosa on an agar plate. Photo: Isaac Miller.
Growing protozoa

Some freshwater protozoans, such as Paramecium aurelia, can be grown in grass soup. Grass soup is made by boiling grass in water, then adding the bacteria, such as Klebsiella aerogenes, as the feed (Fig. 7.8) Growing worms Caenorhabditis elegans, a nematode worm, is used as a model animal for genetic and molecular biology research. The organism can be grown on an E. coli lawn on an agar plate. The worm grows by feeding on bacteria (Fig. 7.8). Growing bacterial viruses Phages harvested from municipal wastewater infect bacterial cells. Wastewater is centrifuged to remove cellular debris and particulates, then filtered through a 0.45-micron filter. The filtrate (about 100 microliters) is mixed with 0.1 ml of a healthy bacterial culture in the presence of 0.1 M MgSO4 (which allows the phages to settle on the bacterial cells). The mixture is added to 3 ml of molten soft agar medium (0.6% agar) and plated onto a nutrient agar plate. The bacterium grows, creating a lawn; the phage kills bacteria in some areas of the lawn, leaving empty spaces called plaques (Fig. 7.8). It is assumed that each plaque is formed by a single phage particle, or more precisely, a plaque- forming unit (pfu). The plaque count can be used to determine the concentration of phage particles in the original wastewater sample that are capable of infecting the bacterial species.
Microbiologists may need to know how many bacteria, virus particles, or white blood cells are in a 1 mL sample. There are many methods for enumerating microbes. Here are a few examples.
Direct counting

A Petroff-Hausser or CellometerTM counting chamber (a glass slide with a small chamber and grids etched on its bottom) can be used to count cells directly. A dilute sample is placed in the chamber under a cover slip, then examined with a light microscope. The number of cells on the grids is counted, and then a formula (specific for the slide used) gives the cell count/ml of sample. For bacterial cells, both live and dead cells are counted. In counting human cells, a dye (trypan blue) is added to the cell solution to stain dead cells blue, allowing only live cells to be counted (Fig. 7.9).
Fig. 7.9. Counting mammalian cells using a Cellometer™. A. The structure of a Cellometer. B. The counting area

of the Cellometer. One of the four counting areas is indicated by a red square. C. Cells in one of the four counting areas are shown. Images B and C are from Electron Microscopy Sciences, Hatfield, Pennsylvania.

Counting live bacteria by the serial dilution method The bacteria sample is serially diluted (Fig. 7.10), and then 0.1 ml of the diluted sample is plated on agar plates. The number of colonies on the plate, ranging from 10 to 300, is counted. The number of bacteria in the original sample is calculated as colony-forming units (cfu) using the formula N= nx10 x dilution factor, where N is the cfu/eml of the original sample, n is the number of colonies on a plate, and 10 is to compensate for the 0.1 ml sample used for plating. Suppose the sample was diluted 10,000-fold and the colony counts on the plate were 45. The cfu/ml of the original sample N= 45x10x10,000= 4.5x106 cfu/ml. A similar method is used to count bacteriophages through the plaque assay described previously.

Counting live bacterial cells in a sample using filter papers If the bacterial count is low (as in clear pond water), a large sample (say 100 mL) is filtered through sterile filter paper. If the bacterial count is high, the sample is diluted before filtration. The filter paper retains bacterial cells on its surface. The filter paper is then placed on a blood agar plate and incubated for 20 hours to allow the bacteria to form colonies (Fig. 7.10). The colony count gives the live bacterial count per mL of water sample.
Indirect counting

Direct microbe counting is often too cumbersome and even unnecessary. A fair estimate by some alternative methods is sufficient for most practical purposes. There are many ways to get a fair estimate of the microbe concentration in a sample. Some of the methods are briefly described here.
Automatic counting devices (Coulter counter)

A Coulter counter counts both viable and non-viable cells as well as particles such as debris and dust particles. The cells, diluted in a liquid, pass through a very narrow channel of the apparatus in a single file (Fig. 7.11). The counter detects changes in the channel's electrical conductance. Because cells are poor electrical conductors, each cell passing through the channel generates a signal. The counter may also determine the size range of the particles. The cell count is displayed on the apparatus's liquid crystal display.
Fig. 7.10. Estimating the number of viable bacteria. A. A urine sample was serially diluted by mixing 1 ml of urine

(or urine-nutrient broth mixture) with 9 ml of nutrient broth; 0.1 ml of the diluted sample was plated on a blood agar plate (in duplicates). To reduce sampling errors, plates with too many or too few colonies are ignored; dilutions that yield a significant colony count (i.e., 10-300 colonies on a 10 cm plate) are used to estimate colony counts. B. Estimating the number of viable bacteria in a sample containing very few bacteria. 100 ml of lake water was filtered using a 0.2-micron filter paper, and the filter paper was pressed over an EMB agar plate. The filter paper was removed, and the plate was incubated at 20oC overnight. The colonies that grew were counted. Since 121 colonies grew on the plate, the bacterial count was 121 cfu/100 mL, or about 1.2 cfu/mL. Image courtesy: Microbenotes.com. Turbidity measurement When cells (or other particulate matter) are present in a fluid, the fluid scatters light more strongly than the pure fluid. A rough estimate of the bacterial cells in a culture broth can be obtained by comparing the degree of light scattering in the culture broth with that of a sterile sample of the same medium.

A simple spectrometer can be used for this purpose. The scattering of visible light (i.e., wavelength 600 nm) by 1 ml of the sterile culture medium is set as the background (i.e., 0 scattering). The degree of light scattering by 1 ml of the bacterial culture (grown in the same culture medium) gives a rough estimate of the cell concentration (Fig. 7.11). For Escherichia coli growing in LB broth, an A600 value of 0.2-0.9 indicates that the bacterium is in the log phase of growth. An A600 value >1.0 indicates that the cell population is in the stationary phase.
Wet or dry weight

If one is growing a very large batch of cells (for protein or nucleic acid extraction, for example), the wet or dry weight of the harvested cells could give an estimate of the cell mass. The cells are pelleted by centrifugation, and the supernatant is removed. The wet weight of the pellet is the difference between the weight of the empty tube and the weight of the tube containing the pellet. The tube can be placed in a desiccator to evaporate the liquid before weighing it to obtain the dry weight of the cells.
Fig. 7.11. Indirect methods for estimating microbial counts. A. A Coulter counter counts cells (or particles) as the

particle (suspended in liquid) passes through a hole (indicated by an arrow) and thereby disturbs the electric conductance of the liquid. The disturbance events are counted and displayed by an attached device. B. Bacterial growth changes the color and consistency of the culture broth. Here, two cuvettes show sterile culture medium (left) and bacterial growth in the same medium (right). C. A simple spectrometer that measures the light scattering of bacterial cells in a culture medium relative to the sterile culture medium. Visible light passes through a slit, and the light is quantified by a sensor. A tube of sterile medium is used to calibrate the spectrometer before the spectrometer measures the light scattered by a tube containing a bacterial culture.

Part 2: Disinfection, antisepsis, and personal protection To prevent contamination, spoilage, and infections, microbes must be removed or reduced in abundance from various products and surfaces. This section discusses controlling microbial growth in laboratory and health care settings, emphasizing disinfection, antisepsis, and personal protection. This discussion may or may not be relevant for open environments, industries, and agriculture.
Important terminologies
Different situations call for different levels of microbial removal. Microbiologists use specific terms (Table 7.4) to describe different degrees of decontamination.
Table 7.4. Terminologies used in sterilization, disinfection, and antisepsis.

Antisepsis Chemical treatment of skin surfaces for reducing microbe counts Cooking Heat-pasteurization to reduce/remove vegetative cells from food Degerming Low-level antisepsis using some chemical agents Disinfection Elimination of microbes from inanimate objects High-level Disinfection (HLD) Inactivating all microbes, including bacterial endospores, from items that cannot be autoclaved (HLD is essentially equivalent to sterilization) Intermediate-level disinfection (ILD) Removing all vegetative cells and viruses from an inanimate object Low-level disinfection (LLD) Cleaning an inanimate object to reduce microbial counts Pasteurization Physical treatments to reduce vegetative microbial cells in a liquid Preservatives Chemicals added to food or medicine to inhibit microbial growth Sanitization LLD of cooking pots and utensils An antimicrobial agent may kill cellular microbes, but the term killing is inappropriate for viruses and subviral agents. We will use the term inactivation to refer to the cessation of all biological activity in cellular organisms, vegetative cells, spores, endospores, acellular microbes, prions, and enzymes.
Specific aims

The goal of infection control is to remove microbes at the desired level using available resources at a reasonable cost. For example, washing can be sufficient for bed linen, but aprons used in the operating theaters require sterilization. To make an informed decision about which treatments to use and the level of disinfection required, one must have a clear understanding of the microbes involved, the materials to be treated, and the end use of the treated materials. The following aspects are especially considered.
Targets of the microbes

A target is an essential microbial component that can be easily and effectively destroyed. The most vulnerable microbial targets are the lipid membrane, enzymes, and the genome. Different antimicrobial agents affect one or more of these targets.
The resilience of the microbes

All microbes are inactivated if the hardiest one is eliminated. The degree of resilience of microbes, from the most durable to the most vulnerable, is generally as follows: The prion agents > bacterial endospores > protozoan cysts > hydrophilic (i.e., the naked) viruses, satellites, and viroids > worm eggs > fungi and fungal spores > vegetative bacterial cells > vegetative protozoan cells > hydrophobic (i.e., the enveloped) viruses and satellites.
Items to be treated

Some items are too large to sterilize, and others are heat-labile; thus, certain disinfection methods are more suitable for treating them. Durable items such as stainless-steel trays can be heat-treated or irradiated; plastic items can be irradiated but not heat-treated. Serum for tissue culture or therapeutic use should be filter-sterilized because heat or chemical treatment would inactivate the proteins. New methods and treatment agents are developed every year, requiring professionals involved in infection control to stay current.
Nature of the environment

Organic substances protect microbes from treatment agents. Thus, a higher level of treatment is required to inactivate microbes in a liter of blood (because of its high protein content) than in a liter of urine (because of its low protein content).
Number of microbes
All factors being equal, the rate of microbe inactivation is a function of time. The higher the concentration of microbes, the longer the treatment must last to inactivate them.
The intensity of exposure and the D value

In general, a short exposure at a high intensity is equivalent to a longer exposure at a lower intensity. Microbes in a unit volume inactivate at a constant rate under constant treatment conditions (say, temperature fixed at 220 ⁰F in a retort).

In the food industry, the decimal reduction time (D value) is used. A D value is defined as the time required to inactivate 90% of the microbes in an item. Thus, each D value reduces the microbial count by one log (Fig. 7.12). If a batch of soup contains 1x104 endospores/gm and the D value at 220⁰C (i.e., D220) is 2 minutes, then it will take six additional minutes of treatment to reduce the endospore count to 1x101. Treatment should continue until the endospore count approaches <1/gm, say 10-6/gm. Such a low count indicates that there would be no more than one endospore in one million grams of the treated food. The D value depends on many factors, including pressure, temperature, and the item's volume.

If the D value is determined at different fixed temperatures and then plotted as a function of temperature, the fitted curve shows a decrease in D value/min with increasing temperature (Fig. 7.12). The slope of the curve is the z value (in minutes). The z value for a particular treatment arrangement helps determine the number of D-value equivalents to apply when a different temperature is used for the treatment.
Fig. 7.12. The D and z values. A. D value. Endospores present in a fixed volume of liquid get inactivated at a constant

rate under fixed treatment conditions (here 240 ⁰F). Here, D240 is one minute; each minute of treatment would reduce the total spore count/mg of food by one log. B. z value. The D values determined at different temperatures are plotted vs. temperature. Note that the D value was reduced from 10 minutes (at 220 oF) to 1 minute (at 240 oF). The slope of the curve (i.e., the z value) is 18 minutes. The z value indicates that if the treatment temperature increases by 18 °F, the treatment time would be reduced by 1 log. Figure adapted from US Food and Drug Administration Inspection Technical Guide.
Risk of infection

Earle Spaulding (1907-1995) grouped objects with a potential risk of infection into three categories (Fig. 7.13): non- critical, semi-critical, and critical items. Items such as the linen and stethoscope cuffs that only touch intact skin are non-critical; items such as the oral spatula that touch intact mucous membranes are semi-critical; and items such as needles and venous catheters that touch sterile tissue and blood are critical. LLD is sufficient for treating noncritical items (ILD is required if the suspected contaminants include highly resilient microbes, such as Mycobacterium sp.). HLD is required to treat most semi-critical and all critical items. Critical items should be enclosed in a pouch impervious to microbes and then sterilized before use.
Fig. 7.13. Critical, semi-critical, and non-critical items. A. Critical items such as surgical scissors are packaged in

breathable but germ-proof pouches and then sterilized. B. Semi-critical items such as endoscopes must undergo HLD treatment and be used immediately before contamination or be encased for future use. C. Non-critical items, such as bedpans, may undergo LLD or ILD treatment based on what type of microbes might have contaminated the items.

sections.heading: Protecting persons and spaces from microbial contamination

blocks.text: Various precautions are taken to protect workers and reduce the possibility of person-to-person, person-to-equipment, and equipment-to-person transmission of pathogens. Some of the general precautions are described below (see also Chapter 5 for aseptic techniques).
Handwashing

According to the CDC, hand washing is a “do-it-yourself (DIY) vaccine.” This statement should be taken seriously because vaccines are the most effective measures of infection control known to humanity. Hands must be washed (a) before and after preparing food; (b) before and after examining patients; (c) after touching garbage, animals, animal food, and animal waste; and (d) after using lavatories and other public spaces, changing diapers, and participating in any other activities that may potentially expose hands to microbes. The CDC recommends the following process for regular hand washing (Fig. 7.14): a) Rinse hands with warm running water.

b) Take a dab of liquid soap and rub on hands (i.e., lather) for at least 20 seconds. Scrub all surfaces (Fig. 7.14), particularly under the fingernails, the spaces between the fingers, and the back of the palm and wrist. c) Rinse hand surfaces well with running water.
d) Dry hands with a clean or disposable towel.
Fig. 7.14. Hand washing. A. Steps of the correct way of handwashing. B. Critical areas of hand surfaces (indicated
by arrows) that may retain microbes if not carefully lathered and washed.

Bar soaps (including antibacterial ones) are not recommended because many microbes grow on them. The liquid soap dispensers should be free of microbial contamination. It is important to lather for 20 seconds. Surveys indicate that people lather their hands for only about 3 seconds. Counting from 1001 to 1020 while rubbing and lathering can ensure 20 seconds of scrubbing.

Clean hands are more prone to microbial contamination than dirty hands. Thus, potentially dirty surfaces should be avoided after rinsing hands. Electric hand dryers can be used only if the machine is in good working condition and equipped with a highly effective particulate (HEPA) filter to remove microbes. Without such a filter, the electric hand dryer would concentrate airborne microbes and deposit them onto the clean hands.

When soap and water are not available or cannot be used, hand sanitizers can be used. The active ingredient of hand sanitizers is usually 70% ethanol or isopropanol in a polyacrylate gel. Some brands may contain mild antibacterial agents such as triclosan or triclocarban, which can be toxic to some people. Hand sanitizers are not an alternative to handwashing. The CDC discourages using hand sanitizers if the hands are visibly dirty.

If one must use hand sanitizer, one should take a large dab of the gel and rub it all over the palm and fingers for at least 20 seconds, until all surfaces are uniformly wet. Wet surfaces must not be wiped with paper towels; rather, the hand should be rubbed until the liquid evaporates.

Regular handwashing is intended to remove environmental microbes from hand surfaces, not the skin's resident microbiota. Medical handwashing for work in operating rooms and emergency rooms requires the use of antimicrobial soap (such as povidone-iodine) and additional scrubbing. Some medical and research protocols also require a shower. Showering and body washing with soap drastically reduce the skin's microbial load and the shedding of dead skin cells and microbes attached to them.
Body coverings

Laboratory and healthcare workers wear clean clothing, body garb over the clothing, gloves, head covers, goggles or full-face covers, and shoe covers (Fig. 7.15) to reduce microbial contamination. Different lab/healthcare-related activities require varying levels of protective coverage.

spaces. Shown is a fully garbed Biocontainment Care Unit nurse of the University of Texas Medical Branch, Houston TX. Image courtesy: Texas Medical Center.

blocks.text: Hospitals and teaching/research laboratories handle many infectious agents. Protecting workers from these agents is a top priority. There are four biosafety levels (BSL) of containment for handling various microbial agents. More information on BSLs can be found at http://www.cdc.gov.
BSL-1 facility

A BSL-1 facility is designed to handle microbes that do not cause disease in healthy humans. A high school biology laboratory is a typical BSL-1 facility. Such a facility is not isolated from the rest of the building. The facility displays appropriate biohazard emblems (Fig. 7.16). Inward airflow (i.e., air entering the laboratory and then leaving through designated air ducts) is preferred but not required. The facility is built from sturdy materials and can be chemically or physically decontaminated if necessary. The facility's benchtops are made of acid-resistant materials. The facility should have hand and eyewash stations and biohazard waste containers. Workers in a BSL-1 facility should have access to laboratory coats, gloves, safety glasses, and mechanical pipetting devices for liquid handling. Mouth- pipetting, eating, drinking, smoking, or storing consumables in such a facility is prohibited. All workers should be trained before being allowed to work in a BSL-1 facility.
BSL-2 facility

A BSL-2 facility may handle certain microbes that can infect healthy subjects, but the agents do not readily aerosolize or are unstable if aerosolized. According to the CDC, appropriately trained personnel may handle prion agents in BSL- 2 containment. Workers should be vaccinated against common blood-borne pathogens. Because there is no vaccine for many infectious microbes, workers should deposit a serum sample for use as a reference should they ever be exposed to an infectious agent. All BSL-1 requirements also apply to BSL-2, except that inward directional airflow is mandatory (Fig. 7.16). All procedures that generate infectious aerosols or splashes should be performed in a Class II biosafety cabinet (BSC II) equipped with a laminar flow hood (Fig. 7.16), where air flows through the base of the cabinet and then passes through a high-efficiency particulate (HEPA) filter. A HEPA filter removes 99.97% of particles larger than 0.3 micrometers. Hazardous wastes should be stored in spill-proof bags and autoclaved before disposal. Used sharp objects should be collected in puncture-resistant canisters. Appropriate regulatory instructions should be posted in the facility. Most college-level and hospital laboratories are BSL-2 facilities.
Fig. 7.16. Hazard emblems and a typical BSL-2 Facility. A. Common hazard emblems displayed in a BSL-2 facility.

Image: Vanderbilt University Medical Center. B. Structure of a BSL-2 facility. 1- Locked door showing hazard emblems; 2- Floor made of monolithic impervious materials; 3a- Chemical hood to handle volatile chemicals; 3b- biological hood; 4- Refrigerators showing the emblem ‘No Food or Drink’; 5- Biohazard waste receptacle with an appropriate emblem; 6- Canister for radioactive waste with an appropriate emblem; 7- Canister to collect sharp objects (it also contains an appropriate emblem but the emblem is not visible in this image); 8- Electric liquid handling devices; 9- Benchtop with acid/base-resistant surface and sinks; 10- Emergency shower head and eyewash station. Image: WHO Biosafety Manual 3rd Ed., 2004.
BSL-3 facility

A BSL-3 facility is required for handling pathogenic microbes that can be aerosolized and cause life-threatening infections. All BSL-1 and BSL-2 requirements apply to BSL-3 facilities. Additional requirements include the following: the facility should be on an isolated floor of a building and equipped with double-door entrances; the wall and roof of the facility should be made of waterproof materials that can be decontaminated readily; the floor should be monolithic (not covered with tiles) and curved four inches up around the wall; the facility should be airtight except that filtered air should flow in the facility and leave through specific vents (without being re-circulated); and the incubators and centrifugation devices that may be used for the facility should be located and operated inside the facility. The incubators and centrifugation devices should suppress aerosol formation.

An entire BSL-3 facility functions as a large biosafety cabinet equipped with HEPA filters. Depending on the microbes used, workers may need to wear a mask or a fully contained respirator suit (Fig. 7.17). Only appropriately trained and experienced workers should be allowed to work at a BSL-3 facility. The hospital's operating rooms (ORs) are maintained as if they were BSL-3 facilities.
Fig. 7.17. Some equipment used in BSL-2, 3, and 4 facilities. A. Workers wearing positive pressure suits before

entering a BSL-4 facility. The tube supplies a steady flow of breathable air and maintains a positive pressure inside the suit to prevent air from the BSL-4 facility from entering. Image courtesy: CDC-PHIL. B. A BSC II type cabinet with stainless-steel and glass walls and a stainless-steel floor. Photo: Ken Slater. C. A laboratory worker using a BSC III. Highly dangerous microbes stored in the cabinet can be handled only through the cabinet's glove boxes. Image courtesy: CDC-PHIL.
BSL-4 facility

A BSL-4 facility provides the highest level of protection for laboratory workers. Pathogenic microbes that are easily aerosolized and cause serious or deadly diseases with no current cure or treatment are handled in BSL-4 facilities. In addition to BSL-3 requirements, BSL-4 facilities require airlocks to prevent microbes from escaping. Air, water, and trash entering a BSL-4 facility must be decontaminated before disposal. In most cases, the entire lab is treated as a large biosafety cabinet. Laboratory work in a BSL-4 facility is performed in a biosafety cabinet (BSC) III, or workers wear a positive-pressure suit (Fig. 7.17) and use a BSC II cabinet. Workers wearing a positive-pressure suit will pass through a chemical shower, then remove the suit and take a personal shower before leaving the facility. Class I, II, and III biosafety cabinets (BSCs) BSC I: A BSC is a contained workspace. The CDC classifies BSCs into three types. All BSCs are laminar-flow hoods with HEPA filters. The hood wall is made of stainless steel and sturdy glass, and the floor is stainless steel as well (Fig. 7.17). The cabinet is equipped with a UV lamp for decontamination. The inward airflow (i.e., speed of the air passing through the hood) for BSC I is 75 feet /min, sufficient to protect workers but not the cells or tissues placed in the cabinet. The air passing through the HEPA filter of a BSC I can be recirculated (i.e., the hood is not ducted). A BSC I is usually used to house centrifuges.

BSC II: There are several types of BSC IIs. The inward airflow rate ranges from 75 to 100 feet/min, and the filtered air can be vented or recirculated within the cabinet. BSC II protects both the workers and the microbial cultures exposed to the cabinet's air.

BSC III: A BSC III is a gas-tight box. Workers may touch materials placed inside the cabinet only through the glovebox (Fig. 7.17). BSL-2 and BSL-3 facilities usually use BSC IIs, and BSL-4 facilities may use BSC IIIs or some types of BSC IIs.

sections.heading: Emergency protocols in case of accidental exposure to infectious agents

blocks.text: Accidental exposure to hazardous microbes may occur even when all routine precautionary protocols are rigorously followed. Some of the common accidents in a healthcare facility or a laboratory are (a) fire, (b) activation of a fire alarm, (c) spill of biohazard materials such as body fluids, tissue culture supernatants, and toxic chemicals, (d) bite or scratch by laboratory animals, (e) personal injuries from contaminated broken glass, sharp objects and hypodermic needles, and (f) burn injuries from splashed chemicals, open flames and exploded cryovials (vials used for storing microbes in liquid nitrogen).

Laboratory and healthcare workers must report all accidents and personal injuries to the facility supervisor. The affected area should be immediately washed with plenty of clean water. Workers should avoid handling hazardous materials after hours without a second person present. In some cases, calling 911 may be necessary. The supervisor should arrange emergency medical care as needed and have the worker provide a blood sample for reference. In general, affected workers are treated for potential pathogens and are monitored periodically for signs of infection and seroconversion related to accidental exposure, in accordance with the regulations of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
