sections.heading: The physical methods of sterilization and disinfection

blocks.text: Sterilization and disinfection methods can be broadly grouped into physical and chemical methods. Physical methods utilize energy and mechanical means, while chemical methods use various chemical substances. Our ancestors used physical methods of infection control, including sunlight for curing and fire for cooking. The major physical methods include heat, electromagnetic radiation, sound waves, high pressure, adsorption, and filtration.

slides.title: Physical Methods: Sound wave and ultrahigh pressure

blocks.text: Heat weakens or breaks chemical bonds and facilitates chemical reactions. Low heat (under 200oC) liquefies membrane lipids and denatures proteins and nucleic acids. High heat (above 200oC) causes combustion, an exothermic reaction between organic substances and oxygen, leading to the formation of carbon dioxide and water. Thermal energy is used in two forms: moist heat and dry heat.
Dry heat

Dry heat is transferred through hot air generated in an oven (Fig. 7.18). Heat transfer through air is inefficient, requiring prolonged treatment at high temperatures and resulting in waste. Biologists sterilize glassware and stainless steelware using this method by heating the items at 200ºC for 2-4 hours to remove RNases, prion agents, and other extremely stable proteins.
Incineration

Many hospitals use large-capacity electric incinerators for the disposal of body parts, animal carcasses, gauges, and some other biohazardous wastes. Incineration is also the method of choice for disposing of large flocks of infected birds. Some municipalities have incinerators for solid waste disposal. Incineration is generally more cost-effective than any other method of decontamination of solid waste. Incineration poses the risk of releasing toxic gases, particulate pollutants, and aerosolized microbes, all of which must be captured. The capture process is technically challenging and expensive. Some microbiologists decontaminate inoculation loops by incinerating them on a Bunsen burner. It may aerosolize microbes, causing an inhalation hazard. A safer alternative is to use an electric loop burner or a disposable loop (Fig. 7.18).
Moist heat

Moist heat is the transfer of heat through steam. Heated water molecules interact with hydrophilic molecules (i.e., proteins and nucleic acids) and rapidly denature them. Thus, moist heat is much more efficient than dry heat of the same temperature and is more cost-effective.
Heat pasteurization

Heat pasteurization is a low-intensity cooking process that inactivates viruses and vegetative cells but not bacterial endospores. It delays spoilage and increases the shelf life of perishable food items. Household open-pot cooking is a form of heat pasteurization. Milk is traditionally pasteurized by heating to 63 °C for 30 minutes. In the high- temperature, short-time (HTST) method, liquid products are heated for only 15 seconds at 72°C. In the ultra-high- temperature (UHT) method, liquid substances are heated for a few seconds at 140-150°C and then rapidly cooled. Vegetative cells and viruses rupture during rapid expansion at 72-150°C. HTST and UHT are extensively used in the food industry, especially in milk processing. Modern laundry machines and clothes dryers essentially heat-pasteurize non-disposable clothes.
Fig. 7.18. Dry heat for sterilization and disinfection. A. A dry-heat oven is used to sterilize laboratory glassware.

B. An electric burner for the heat-sterilization of metal loops. Inset: Disposable sterile plastic loops, a safer alternative to the conventional metal loops. C. Flame of a Bunsen burner. If it must be used for heating inoculation loops, the metal loop should be incinerated at the tip of the flame (indicated by the arrow), where the temperature is most intense. Autoclaving An autoclave (Fig. 7.19) is a sophisticated pressure cooker that can maintain water vapor at 15 pounds per square inch (PSI) pressure and 121 °C. Note that water boils at 100 oC at sea level, where the barometric pressure is one atmosphere (i.e., 14.7 pounds/sq inch or 1013 millibars). The elevated pressure is necessary to increase the steam temperature to 121 °C. If done properly, autoclaving kills/inactivates bacterial endospores and all microbes, although it does not inactivate prion agents and some RNases.
Fig. 7.19. Using an autoclave. A. Structure of an autoclave showing the treatment chamber and steam inlets and

outlets. The temperature gauge and the insulation components are not shown. Image courtesy: scienceabc.com/. EV- exhaust valve, SI- steam inlet, SS- steam supply, WL- steam waste line. B. Liquid substances are autoclaved in heat- tolerant, loosely capped containers, such as Pyrex conical flasks. C. Solid objects are wrapped in microporous paper/plastic pouches) before autoclaving. D. Wrapping with aluminum or ordinary plastic foil may not guarantee sterilization.

Liquid and solid (but not gaseous) items can be autoclaved. Liquid items must be placed in a loosely capped, heat- stable vessel (to prevent explosion and melting). Solid items must also be heat-stable. Autoclaving liquid items involves three steps: conditioning (gradually increasing steam pressure and temperature to prevent rapid expansion and rupture of glass vessels), treatment (maintaining a constant temperature of 121 oC and pressure of 15 PSI for 10- 15 minutes to ensure sterilization), and exhaust (gradually releasing steam pressure to prevent boilover). Solid objects do not require the three steps. The flash autoclaving method reduces the exposure time to 3 minutes by increasing the pressure to 28 PSI and the temperature to 135 oC. To prevent scalding injuries, the autoclave door must not be opened until the exhaust step is complete. Liquid samples (such as bacterial growth media) should be removed soon after the exhaust step is complete to prevent evaporative loss and caramelization.

Objects such as surgical knives must be cleaned to remove any chemical contaminants, washed, and then properly wrapped before autoclaving. The wrap must have microscopic pores through which moisture passes, but microbes cannot. An item would not be sterilized if steam does not come into direct contact with its surfaces. Solid objects wrapped in aluminum foil or ordinary plastic membranes may not be sterilized because the wrapping may lack holes of the appropriate size for steam to enter (Fig. 7.19). There are special paper and plastic wraps for autoclaving surgical instruments.
Quality control for autoclaving

Inadequately autoclaved surgical and other medical equipment has been involved in many fatal microbial infections. To ensure proper functioning, autoclaves should be periodically inspected and serviced by an engineer. When heated, indicator tapes placed on the items to be autoclaved darken (Fig. 7.20). Darkened tapes do not guarantee that the items have been sterilized. Some autoclave models display the operating conditions, which are more reliable than indicator tapes.

A more appropriate test for proper autoclave function is employing the endospore viability test, using commercially available endospores of Bacillus subtilis or Geobacillus stearothermophilus. The endospores are packed into a tube and then placed in an ampule containing bacterial growth medium (Fig. 7.20). The growth medium contains a pH indicator dye to give it a purple color. The ampule is placed in the autoclave (or in the center of a bag full of biohazard waste). After autoclaving, the tube containing the endospores is broken (by tightening the ampule cap) so that the spores are suspended in the medium. For the Pro-Spore test (Mesa BI, Bozeman, MT), the sealed ampule containing the endospores is placed in the autoclave and then incubated at room temperature for 48 hours. If the autoclave had functioned properly, the endospores would have been inactivated, and the medium would have remained purple (Fig.7.20). If the autoclave had malfunctioned, the spores would have germinated. Vegetative bacterial cells would grow in the medium and release lactic acid, changing the medium's color from purple to yellow (Fig. 7.20).
Fig. 7.20. Quality control for autoclave function. A. Indicator tapes show white and beige stripes before heating

and zebra stripes after heating. B. Germination of bacterial endospores in the Pro-Spore test. The autoclaved ampules changing from purple to yellow indicate that the autoclave malfunctioned (sterilization had not been achieved). Image: Midland Scientific Inc.
Decontaminating prion agents

According to the CDC, tissues, cells, and body fluids containing prion agents should be incinerated in an appropriately constructed facility. Glass and metal equipment that contacted prion agents should be immersed in a 1.0 M NaOH solution or a 20,000 ppm sodium hypochlorite solution for 1 hour, then autoclaved for 1 hour at 121 °C. Equipment that contacts brain tissue should be considered potentially contaminated with prion agents and decontaminated accordingly before reuse.
Cryopreservation

Naturally present enzymes in fresh meat, fruits, and vegetables degrade and spoil them even in the absence of microbial growth. Low temperatures slow enzyme activity and microbial growth, thereby slowing food spoilage. This is why perishable items in the households are either refrigerated (stored at 4-8°C) or frozen at -18 oC. According to the FDA, freezing at -4°F or below for 7 days, or freezing at -35°C or below for 15 hours, kills most worms, their eggs, and their larvae, provided the items are less than 6 inches thick. In the United States, meat and seafood consumed raw (such as sushi, sashimi, ceviche, and tartar) must be deep-frozen before serving. Viruses, as well as some bacteria and fungi, may remain viable in freezing conditions. Frozen food can suffer freezer burn (dehydration and oxidation), which alters its consistency and taste, especially when a frost-free freezer is used.

Electromagnetic radiation is waves of photons in an electromagnetic field. All photons travel at 299,792 km/sec but may have different wavelengths. The shorter the wavelength, the higher the wave frequency (number of waves/sec) expressed in Hertz (Hz), and the energy of the radiation (Fig. 7.21). Thus, gamma radiation is more energetic than UV light or visible light. Atoms get excited when they absorb electromagnetic radiation. This has various consequences, including the movement of atoms and the breaking/making of chemical bonds. Thus, light can be used to inactivate microbes. Solar and cosmic radiation contain both high-energy (gamma rays and X-rays) and low-energy (UV light and visible light).
Fig. 7.21. The electromagnetic radiation spectrum. Showing is the range of wavelengths of various forms of light.
Note that the shorter the wavelength, the more energetic and penetrative the radiation. The wave frequency (cycles/sec, in Hz) of different types of radiation is shown at the bottom. Image: NIH.gov.
Ionizing radiation

Cosmic rays, gamma rays, and X-rays are short wavelengths/high-energy radiation (Fig. 7.21). Many radioisotopes, including Cobalt-60 and Cesium-137, emit gamma rays. X-rays are produced by bombarding metallic lenses with electrons. Gamma rays and X-rays are classified as ionizing radiation because atoms may lose electrons and become ionized upon absorbing them. Since water is the most abundant chemical in the cell, they absorb most of the radiation and undergoes radiolysis.

H2O (ionizing radiation) à H2O+ + e- (electron) H2O+ soon breaks, and the e- reacts with water, initiating a chain reaction that creates many reactive chemical species, including hydroxyl free radicals (OH-), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and superoxide (O2-). These chemical species may react with macromolecules such as DNA, RNA, and proteins, altering them. Gamma rays and X-rays may also directly break DNA and RNA. Broken DNA cannot be replicated, broken mRNA cannot be translated, and altered proteins may lose enzyme activities, all of which contribute to cell death.

Gamma radiation (emitted by radioisotopes such as Cobalt-60 or Cesium-137) is widely used to sterilize heat-sensitive materials, such as disposable plastic medical devices and surgical supplies. Dry food products and spices are also sterilized by gamma irradiation. The FDA has recently approved gamma irradiation for sterilizing and pasteurizing wet food items such as meat and dairy products. Gamma irradiation may affect the flavor of some food items; however, these approved methods are safe. Many of the NASA and US military food rations are sterilized by gamma irradiation. Gamma irradiation treatment is usually performed in a dedicated plant designed for continuous operation (Fig. 7.22). Materials to be irradiated are packed in cartons and then conveyed to the plant for irradiation. A drawback is that gamma irradiation facilities generate hazardous waste that is difficult and expensive to dispose of. Electron beam (E-beam) The E-beam is generated in a cathode-ray tube. The electrons are then accelerated by a high-power linear accelerator. High-velocity electrons are used to sterilize medical equipment made of plastic, paper, and cloth (Fig. 7.22). E-beams, like gamma radiation, are ionizing radiation. E-beam is less penetrating than gamma irradiation, but E-beam sterilizes faster (in about a minute) than gamma irradiation (which takes several hours). Like a gamma radiation facility, E- beam sterilization requires the setup of a plant for continuous operation (Fig. 7.22). E-beam treatment does not produce potentially hazardous chemicals within the treated products. However, E-beam is not used to sterilize food substances.
Fig. 7.22. Gamma irradiation and E-Beam facilities. A. A gamma radiation station. Gamma rays from a Cobalt-60

source are used to irradiate items (including food). B. An E-beam irradiation station. The high-speed electrons pass through a metal window and enter the packages containing the items to be treated. The items are placed on a conveyor belt to transport them to the treatment chamber. Images are adapted from the Center for Consumer Research, UC Davis.

Non-ionizing radiation UV light UV radiation is often divided into UVA (wavelength 315-400 nm), UVB (wavelength 280-315 nm), and UVC (wavelength 100-280 nm) based on their wavelengths and the extent to which the ozone layer in the upper atmosphere absorbs them. The ozone layer does not absorb UVA radiation, partially absorbs UVB radiation, and completely absorbs UVC radiation from incoming solar radiation.

UVB radiation coming through the ozone layer can cause skin cancer if one is exposed to intense solar radiation. UVC generated by mercury lamps may ionize water molecules, acting like ionizing radiation. High doses of UVA and UVB cross-link DNA, RNA, and proteins, inactivating them (Fig. 7.23). UV rays do not penetrate well and therefore have only limited applications in controlling microbes. UVC is used to treat drinking water, fruit juice, and alcoholic beverages (in thin films), and to decontaminate air and the surfaces of operating rooms and safety cabinets.
Fig. 7.23. The mode of action of ionizing radiation and short-wave UV radiation. A. Ionizing radiation, such as

gamma-ray, X-Ray, E-beam, and UVC, ionizes molecules, including water molecules, and creates reactive chemicals. Reactive chemicals bind to and break DNA (and RNA, not shown). B. A normal DNA molecule with two adjacent thymine residues. C. DNA molecules with UV-induced cross-links. UVA and UVB rays activate C atoms of the bases, causing unnatural covalent bonds (cross-links, shown by the red lines).
Microwave ovens

Microwave ovens use a magnetron to generate relatively long-wave (wavelength ~12.2 cm) electromagnetic radiation (Fig. 7.24). When a microwave oven is on, the electric field inside it reverses direction repeatedly at very high speed, causing water molecules in food to rotate rapidly and generate intense heat. Heat distribution in the commonly available microwave ovens is non-uniform because microwaves penetrate different materials at different rates. One region of microwave-treated frozen meat may remain ice-cold while the other part of the same item may be burned. Therefore, microwave ovens fail to uniformly inactivate microbes. Microwave ovens can be used for warming food, not for conventional disinfection/cooking.
Fig. 7.24. Use of non-ionizing radiation in inactivating microbes. A. Structure of a microwave oven; a- transformer,

b- filter, c- capacitor, d- magnetron, e- waveguide, f- mode stirrer, g- control panel, h- turntable, i- food item to be warmed, j- water molecules inside the food item, k- the rapid shifting in the polarity of the wave field. The mode stirrer and turntable strive to distribute the microwave energy uniformly. The oven generates intense heat due to the rapid rotation of water molecules (and friction among them) in response to the rapid shift in the electric field's polarity. B. Use of diode laser in treating periodontal infections. The laser serves as an adjunct in eradicating bacteria that cause periodontitis. Image from Lobo TM, Pol DG. J Indian Soc Periodontology 2015; 19(1): 43-48.
Laser

Light from a light bulb is blackbody radiation, consisting of light of many different wavelengths. The waves of such light are unsynchronized and deflect in many directions. A laser consists of photons released by excited electrons in an atom. The photons have a single wavelength, and the waves are synchronized and directional. Laser beams can be made very thin, sharp, and extremely powerful. Lasers can be used to cut live tissues during surgery, cauterize inflamed tissues, and inactivate microbes present in live tissues (Fig. 7.24).

Sound is the oscillation of pressure, stress, or displacement of particles in a solid, liquid, or gaseous medium. Sound waves with frequencies above the audible range are ultrasonic. Ultrasonic sound waves (20-40 kHz/sec) create miniature bubbles in a fluid. The process is called cavitation. Microbubbles form within the cytoplasm of a cell exposed to ultrasonic sound waves. The bubbles subsequently collapse, creating a shock wave that damages the cell by disrupting the plasma membrane. The shock wave may release heat, detach molecules from hard surfaces, and break larger molecules into fragments. Sonicators (used to make cell extracts) break bacterial cells through cavitation. Ultrasonic baths (Fig. 7.25) are used to clean the surfaces of surgical equipment before the items are washed and autoclaved. Cavitation technologies for cleaning water and pasteurizing eggs have also been developed.
Fig. 7.25. Use of sound waves and pressure in inactivating microbes. A. An ultrasonic bath is a common sight in

a hospital. The bath contains a fluid through which sonar pulses (sound waves) travel. Metallic surgical instruments are decontaminated in the sonic bath. B. Ultra-high-pressure chambers are used in cold pasteurizing fruit juice. The process denatures proteins and lipids, thereby inactivating microbes.

High-pressure processing (HPP) involves applying up to 100,000 bars to pasteurize foods such as guacamole and fruit juices (Fig. 7.25). The high pressure presumably denatures proteins and affects membrane properties. The process, also called hyperbaric (or cold) pasteurization, inactivates microbial cells and increases the shelf life of the treated food without destroying its delicate flavor.

Filtration is the use of absorbent surfaces (i.e., matrix filters) or physical sieves (i.e., size-exclusion filters) to remove particles suspended in gases or liquids. The matrix filter holds (adsorbs) the molecules to be removed (the molecules bind and form a film on the matrix filter). Some matrix filters, such as activated charcoal filters (Fig. 7.26), also adsorb soluble substances and suspended particles from air and water.
Size-exclusion filters

Size-exclusion filters have a nominal (average) pore size or cutoff limit that allows smaller particles and the medium (solvent or air) to pass through, while retaining larger particles (Fig. 7.26). Various types of inert organic fibers (cellulose, polysulfone, polycarbonate, and nylon) are used to make the size-exclusion filters. Filters with 0.1-0.2 micrometer nominal pore size remove all cellular microbes. However, filters with a nominal pore size of 0.40 microns or higher may not retain bacterial cells of the genera Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma (because they lack cell walls) and spirochetes (because they are 0.35 microns in width).

Commonly used size-exclusion filtration devices do not remove virus particles. Air in a laminar-flow hood is filtered by HEPA filters. HEPA filters have a cutoff of 0.3 micrometers. Narrower pores limit airflow, but a pump can increase the flow rate. Drinking water in some municipalities is filtered through gravel-and-sand filters. Groundwater is naturally purified as rainwater passes through many layers of microporous rocks.
Ultrafiltration

Ultrafiltration also uses size-exclusion filters, but the membranes have a nominal pore size of 0.0001- 0.1 micrometers, capable of retaining molecules as small as NaCl dissolved in water. Reagent-grade water is produced from tap water, and drinking water is produced from seawater using ultrafiltration. The ultrafiltration membrane quickly becomes fouled due to the deposition of solute molecules on the surface. The membrane is constantly cleaned by bubbling gas to increase the flow rate (Fig. 7.26).
Fig. 7.26. Filtration and ultrafiltration. A. A matrix filter adsorbs particulate matter or soluble contaminants from

a solvent. A household water filter unit containing a cartridge packed with activated carbon particles is shown. B. A size-exclusion filter. A negative pressure is applied to the device to increase the flow rate. Inset: A SEM image of the filter's pores created by many layers of cellulose or nylon fibers. C. Ultrafiltration. Shown is the PruronTM filtering device (Koch, Wilmington, MA) that uses hollow fibers. Negative pressure draws water molecules into the hollow fibers but excludes larger molecules, such as NaCl. The collected water is removed at the base. Air bubbles are constantly pushed through the column to clean the hollow fibers. Figure courtesy http://www.kochmembrane.com/.

sections.heading: Chemical methods of sterilization and disinfection

blocks.text: Thousands of brands of antimicrobial chemicals are available for household, hospital, municipal, and industrial use. Several factors are considered in selecting a chemical antimicrobial agent. An ideal antimicrobial chemical should have most of the following characteristics: a) highly effective at reasonably low concentrations b) nontoxic and noncarcinogenic c) cost-effective in manufacturing, transportation, storage, and field applications d) not easily altered to hazardous chemicals such as explosives and poisons e) non-reactive and non-corrosive f) does not produce hazardous degradation byproducts g) biodegradable, but it has a reasonable shelf life h) effective concentration does not change during its shelf life None of the available antimicrobial chemicals has all the ideal properties, but different groups of chemicals have specific applications. The commonly used groups of antimicrobial chemicals are described here in alphabetical order. Alcohols Alcohols are chaotropic agents (chemicals that disrupt hydrogen bonding) that denature proteins and are effective against enveloped viruses, many species of bacteria (vegetative), and fungi and fungal spores. Water enhances protein- alcohol interactions, thereby increasing efficacy. Thus, 75-91 % ethanol is more effective than pure (i.e., 100% or 200 proof) ethanol. However, some bacteria, including Pseudomonas aeruginosa may grow inside diluted (<50%) ethanol. Mouthwashes contain about 27% ethanol and should be protected from bacterial contamination. Recent reports indicated that alcohol-containing mouthwashes may increase the risk of oral cancers. Prolonged exposure to isopropanol vapor has also been linked to neurological damage and nasal cancers. Other common alcohols, such as methanol, phenol, and ethylene glycol, have similar biological activities, but they cannot be used because they are toxic to humans.
Aldehydes

Formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde, and ortho-phthalaldehyde inactivate microbes by cross-linking the –NH2, –OH, – COOH, —SH functional groups of the macromolecules (Fig. 7.27). Formalin (a 37% aqueous solution of formaldehyde) is used to preserve biological samples such as stools, tissue sections, and cadavers. Alkaline 2.0% glutaraldehyde solution is a sterilant (used for HLD); it inactivates vegetative cells in 10 minutes and endospores in 10-12 hours. Both formaldehyde and glutaraldehyde are carcinogens; thus, treated surfaces must be thoroughly rinsed in sterile distilled water before use.
Fig. 7.27. Aldehydes, biguanides, and epoxides. A. Formaldehyde and how it cross-links. Shown is the crosslinking

reaction of two NH2 groups by a formaldehyde molecule. B. Chlorhexidine, a biguanide, works by disrupting the lipid membranes. C. Ethylene oxide (an epoxide) and how it cross-links. The crosslinking reaction of two NH2 groups by a molecule of ethylene oxide is illustrated.
Biguanides

Biguanides (Fig. 7.27) inactivate some bacteria by disrupting the lipid membranes and binding to the cell wall. Some biguanides, such as chlorhexidine, can be toxic (they may cause deafness if applied to the middle ear). Chlorhexidine is effective against some bacteria and viruses. Chlorhexidine digluconate (0.2%) is used in mouthwashes, topical skin cleansers, and swimming pools. Biguanides are more effective in controlling G(+) bacteria than G(-) bacteria. However, the agent's effective concentration is essentially ineffective against most fungi, some bacterial genera (such as Pseudomonas sp.), and endospores. Many nosocomial (hospital-acquired) bacterial infections start with contaminated mouthwash containing biguanides as preservatives.
Epoxides

Similar to aldehydes, epoxides (such as ethylene oxide and propylene oxide gases) inactivate microbes by cross- linking the –NH2, –OH, –COOH, –SH functional groups of the macromolecules (Fig. 7.27). Ethylene oxide (gas) can be used to sterilize heat-labile objects such as pacemakers. The gases are highly toxic (potentially carcinogenic) and flammable. Objects must be treated for about 10 hours at a specific temperature and humidity, and the treated objects must be detoxified for 12 hours before use.
Halogens

Four elements of the Periodic Table group 17 (i.e., F, Cl, Br, and I) are collectively called the halogens. Halogen ions (for example, F- and Cl-) are strong reducing agents, while molecular halogens (such as Cl2 and F2) and many of their compounds are powerful oxidizing agents.

Fluorine is excessively reactive and is not used. A small amount of sodium monophosphofluoride (NaFPO4) is added to the municipal water supply in some states and to toothpaste. Fluoride reacts with tooth enamel, preventing tooth decay. Fluoridation of water has no antimicrobial effect.

Bromine is the most stable and least irritating halogen. It is used to decontaminate and preserve swimming pools and hot spas. However, bromine is relatively expensive. Iodine is nontoxic at some concentrations, quite stable, and relatively inexpensive. Households, municipalities, hospitals, and industries extensively use various compounds of chlorine and iodine.
Chlorine compounds

Chlorine works by oxidizing proteins and inactivating enzymes. The commonly used chlorines include elemental chlorine (Cl2), sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl2), bleaching powder (a mixture of CaOCl2, CaCl2, and CaO2Cl2), chloramine (NH2Cl), and chlorine oxide (ClO2) gas (Fig. 7.28). The availability of molecular chlorine in the solution determines the effectiveness of the products. A basic pH and the presence of organic substances that absorb Cl- ions reduce the effectiveness of chlorine products. A mere one part per million (ppm) of chlorine may inactivate bacteria and viruses suspended in liquid. Chlorine ions are consumed rapidly. Therefore, higher concentrations of hypochlorite or less chemically active alternatives, such as chloramines, are used for municipal water treatment.
Fig. 7.28. Some antimicrobial halogen compounds. A. Sodium hypochlorite and chloramine are used in water

treatment. B. Clorox®, a brand of Clorox Co (Oakland, CA), is a 6% sodium hypochlorite solution. C. Trihalomethane is a toxic byproduct of chlorine, generated in chlorinated water that contains decayed organic substances. D. Povidone- iodine, such as Betadine® (a trademark of Mundipharma, Cambridge, MA), is as effective as tincture of iodine but much less irritating.

Tap water contains about 0.5 ppm of chlorine, not enough to inactivate protozoan cysts, bacterial endospores, and some naked viruses. Clorox (6% sodium hypochlorite solution) is a commonly used household disinfectant. A 10% Clorox solution may effectively inactivate all viruses and bacterial cells in a few minutes. Chlorine reacts with certain suspended organic chemicals to produce toxic and repugnant byproducts, such as trihalomethanes (THMs), including dibromochloromethane (Fig. 7.28). THMs cause liver, kidney, and central nervous system damage. The Florida Department of Health limits THM concentrations in drinking water to <80 micrograms/liter. Concentrated chlorine solutions are toxic, corrosive, irritating, and smelly.
Iodine compounds

Iodine, like chlorine, is an oxidizing agent that presumably reacts with the tyrosine residues and inactivates enzymes. Iodine inactivates vegetative cells but not endospores. Iodine, unlike chlorine, is non-corrosive and can be used as an antiseptic to clean the doctor’s hands and the patient’s body surfaces before surgery. Tincture of iodine (a 2% solution of iodine and sodium iodide in ethanol) is an effective disinfectant but is highly irritating and may stain fabrics. Iodophors are agents formed by attaching iodine atoms to a carrier molecule, such as polyvinylpyrrolidone. Iodophors are non-irritating, do not stain clothing, and release more free iodine ions than tinctures. Povidone-iodine, an iodophor, is commonly used in households (Fig. 7.28). However, some bacteria, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, may grow in iodophor preparations.
Metal compounds

Many metal salts dissolve in water, releasing cations. The cations are powerful oxidizing agents. They react with cellular molecules, inactivating them. Metal salts may readily inactivate vegetative cells but not necessarily the endospores. The effective antimicrobial concentration of the metal ions is toxic to humans and potentially damaging to treated surfaces. Therefore, metal salts are rarely used.

The two most commonly used metal salts are copper sulfate (CuSO4) and silver nitrate (AgNO3). Bordeaux mixture, an aqueous solution of Ca(OH)2 and CuSO4 (1.0% each), is an effective antifungal agent used to prevent fungal infections of grape plants. However, it is highly toxic to animals, including humans and algae. A dilute CuSO4 solution (about 0.1 mg/liter) is highly effective in controlling algal blooms in ponds and lakes.

In the past, dilute solutions of silver nitrate (AgNO3) (about 0.1 mg/liter) were used as eye drops to prevent neonatal eye infections. At present, antibiotic eye drops are used instead. Silver-impregnated catheters and kitchen countertops retard microbial growth.

Alum (a mixture of aluminum sulfate and sulfates of several other elements, including potassium and sodium) is used as an astringent. Alum causes suspended particles and bacterial cells in water to flocculate and precipitate. Green vitriol (FeSO4, nH20) can also be used as a flocculating agent. These agents are used in water purification (see Chapter 15).
Ozone and other peroxygens

Ozone (O3) is an unstable form of molecular oxygen (Fig. 7.29). Peroxygens are compounds containing excess or readily removable oxygen atoms. Ozone and peroxygens are highly reactive and powerful oxidizing agents. They inactivate microbes by reacting with cellular macromolecules. Commonly used peroxygens include hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), benzoyl peroxide ([C6H5C(O)]2O2), peracetic acid (CH3CO3H), and sodium perborate (Na2H4B2O8). Peroxygens can be used as sterilants, but they are unstable and must be synthesized in situ. Ozone gas is used for drinking water treatment.

Hydrogen peroxide gas is used for decontaminating food containers because the gas is non-corrosive and does not produce toxic byproducts. Hydrogen peroxide (3-6% in water) and benzoyl peroxide (2.5-10.0%) are used as antiseptic agents, particularly in washing wounds and acne.

A 0.2% peracetic acid solution can be used to rapidly sterilize solid surfaces. Peracetic acid is toxic and lethal at concentrations of 1.5 ppm or higher. Peroxygens release nascent oxygen atoms that bleach colored substances. Thus, peroxygens are often used in bleaching fabrics, paper, and hair.

Sodium perborate is used in laundry detergents and some whitening toothpastes, but its primary purpose is bleaching, not disinfection. Peroxides are irritants and potentially carcinogenic at high concentrations and with prolonged exposure.

Phenol and phenolics

Phenolics (or phenols) are aromatic hydrocarbons with one or more –OH functional groups directly attached to the benzene ring. Phenol, also called carbolic acid (Fig. 7.29), is the simplest of the phenols. Phenol was the antiseptic Joseph Lister (1827-1912) used in the 1850s, a discovery that revolutionized surgery. Phenol dissolves lipid membranes and denatures proteins in vegetative cells, but some naked viruses and endospores are resistant to phenol. Phenol is highly pungent, caustic, expensive, and unstable at room temperature.

Some phenolics are less pungent, inexpensive, and more effective than phenol. Hexachlorophene, once a widely used phenolic, is currently not used because it is neurotoxic and potentially mutagenic and teratogenic (may cause birth defects) at high concentrations. Triclosan, another phenolic, was once used in soap and dentifrices (Fig. 7.29), but the FDA has found it ineffective.

Capsaicin, the chemical compound that makes hot chili peppers, is a phenolic compound. Capsaicin is occasionally used as a biodegradable pesticide. Some nontoxic phenolics, such as triclosan (Fig. 7.29) and thymol, are added to personal care products, including soaps and toothpaste. Menthol, another phenolic compound, is used in candies and cough syrups. Most of the phenolics are modestly effective antimicrobial agents.
Soaps and detergents

Soaps are sodium or potassium salts of naturally occurring fatty acids (Fig. 7.30). Detergents are synthetic petrochemicals with a hydrocarbon tail and a polar head group (Fig. 7.30). Soaps and some detergents have little antimicrobial activity, but they are surfactants (enhance the cleaning power of water). When dissolved in water, surfactants reduce the surface tension of water. As a result, soapy water interacts more strongly with surfaces and penetrates small cracks and crevices (Fig. 7.30).

Unlike soaps, some detergents are non-biodegradable. Non-biodegradable detergents released by households and industries may accumulate in lakes and rivers, polluting water bodies. Soaps are less effective in hard water (water containing dissolved minerals such as calcium and magnesium sulfates). Detergents are unaffected by water hardness because they do not interact with metal ions as soaps do. Both soaps and detergents have hydrophobic tails that interact with grease and oils, helping to clean oily surfaces.

Detergents can be non-ionic, anionic, cationic, and zwitterionic. Nonionic detergents have a polar head group that does not dissociate. Detergents used for dishwashing are nonionic because they do not foam. Some nonionic detergents, such as Nonidet P-40 (Fig. 7.30) and Triton X-100, are used in protein extraction because they may disrupt membranes and lyse cells without denaturing proteins.

Anionic detergents have a sulfate, sulfonate, or similar negatively charged head group. Anionic detergents, such as sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), are excellent cleaners and produce abundant foam (Fig. 7.30). SDS also disrupts lipid membranes and completely denatures proteins. The polar end of some cationic detergents contains a positively charged quaternary ammonium ion. These detergents, called quats, may inactivate vegetative cells and enveloped viruses by interacting with lipid membranes. Some quats, such as benzalkonium chloride, are non-toxic to humans. Benzalkonium chloride is used in personal hygiene products such as oral rinses and eye drops, but some bacteria, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, may grow in quats. Zwitterionic detergents have both positively and negatively charged polar groups. CHAPS, a zwitterionic detergent, disrupts lipid membranes to extract membrane proteins. Laundry detergents contain nonionic and anionic surfactants, as well as various additives. Major additives include water softeners (such as EDTA), bleaches (such as sodium hypochlorite), enzymes (such as fungal proteases), antifoaming agents (such as silica), lubricants (such as sodium silicate), fabric softeners (such as quats, to reduce static electricity in dried clothes), and perfumes. Beyond bleach and quats, the ingredients of conventional laundry detergents have little overall antimicrobial activity. Clothes washed in cold water with conventional laundry detergents retain many microbes. Items contaminated with high concentrations of microbes should be sorted and washed separately. Modern high-temperature washers remove more microbes.

Dishwasher detergents usually contain nonionic detergents, chlorine bleach, lubricants, and perfumes. Because a dishwasher operates at a higher temperature, washed dishes are much cleaner than clothes washed using a laundry machine.
Chemical preservatives

Chemical preservatives are added to food, beverages, medicines, vaccines, and cosmetics to prevent microbial growth and undesirable chemical changes. An ideal preservative should be stable, non-reactive, non-toxic, non-carcinogenic, water-soluble, and effective. Highly toxic preservatives such as thiomersal (a mercury compound) were used in the past. Much safer alternatives are available today, but an ideal preservative has yet to be developed.
